claim: Intelligent behavior requires acting directed by goals despite competing action tendencies triggered by stimuli in the environment.
source: Intelligent behavior requires to act directed by goals despite competing action tendencies triggered by stimuli in the environment.
evidence: This is a foundational statement drawing from established scientific understanding of goal-directed behavior and cognitive control.

claim: For eye movements, the ability to act goal-directed is briefly reduced in urgent situations.
source: For eye movements, it has recently been discovered that this ability is briefly reduced in urgent situations (Salinas et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Salinas et al., 2019.

claim: In a time-window before an urgent response, participants could not help but look at a suddenly appearing visual stimulus, even though their goal was to look away from it.
source: In a time-window before an urgent response, participants could not help but look at a suddenly appearing visual stimulus, even though their goal was to look away from it.
evidence: This describes findings from Salinas et al., 2019, as indicated by the preceding citation.

claim: Urgency provokes a period in which saccadic eye movements are dominated by external stimuli and uncontrollable by current goals.
source: Urgency seemed to provoke a new visual–oculomotor phenomenon: A period in which saccadic eye movements are dominated by external stimuli, and uncontrollable by current goals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of findings from Salinas et al., 2019, based on the preceding context.

claim: The period of stimulus-dominated saccadic eye movements was assumed to arise from brain mechanisms controlling eye movements and spatial attention, such as those of the frontal eye field.
source: This period was assumed to arise from brain mechanisms controlling eye movements and spatial attention, such as those of the frontal eye field.
evidence: This describes an assumption from prior work (Salinas et al., 2019) about the neural mechanisms underlying the phenomenon.

claim: In well-investigated manual tasks, urgency made goal-conflicting stimulus features dominate behavioral responses.
source: We found that also in well-investigated manual tasks, urgency made goal-conflicting stimulus features dominate behavioral responses.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by experimental data from Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: The dominance of behavior by stimulus features followed established trial-to-trial signatures of cognitive control mechanisms that replicate across a variety of tasks.
source: This dominance of behavior followed established trial-to-trial signatures of cognitive control mechanisms that replicate across a variety of tasks.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing trial-to-trial sequence effects in both experiments.

claim: Urgency temporarily forces stimulus-driven action by overcoming cognitive control in general, not only at brain mechanisms controlling eye movements.
source: Thus together, these findings reveal that urgency temporarily forces stimulus-driven action by overcoming cognitive control in general, not only at brain mechanisms controlling eye movements.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by data from both experiments showing effects in manual tasks.

claim: Brain mechanisms for cognitive control enable goal-directed behavior even when overcoming compelling tendencies for other behaviors.
source: This requires brain mechanisms for cognitive control, which enable to behave goal directed even if this means to overcome compelling tendencies for other behaviors (Cohen, 2017; Egner and Hirsch, 2005; Gratton et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature on cognitive control.

claim: Brain mechanisms for cognitive control are assumed to be implemented in the frontal cortex.
source: These brain mechanisms are assumed to be implemented in the frontal cortex (Miller, 2000; Nee and D'Esposito, 2016; Ridderinkhof et al., 2004; Tang et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to neuroscience literature.

claim: Devastating impairments of goal-directed behavior occur in neurological disorders with frontal damages.
source: which is evident from the devastating impairments of goal-directed behavior in neurological disorders with frontal damages (Alexander et al., 2007; Badre et al., 2009; Casey et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical neuroscience literature.

claim: Brain mechanisms for cognitive control interface with attention mechanisms at multiple levels of processing.
source: The brain mechanisms for cognitive control are thought to interface with attention mechanisms at multiple levels of processing (e.g., Egner, 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Egner, 2008.

claim: Cognitive control mechanisms enforce that goal-relevant information is prioritized, whereas conflicting information is rejected.
source: thereby enforcing that goal-relevant information is prioritized, whereas conflicting information is rejected (Cohen, 2017; Gratton et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cohen, 2017 and Gratton et al., 2017.

claim: Salinas et al., 2019 found that the need for urgent responding opened up a time-window of approximately 40 ms in which the ability to perform goal-directed saccadic eye movements was severely reduced.
source: Salinas et al., 2019 found that the need for urgent responding opened up a time-window (~40 ms) in which the ability to perform goal-directed saccadic eye movements was severely reduced.
evidence: This is a specific finding from Salinas et al., 2019, as indicated by the citation.

claim: In antisaccade tasks, participants have to look away from a suddenly appearing visual stimulus, which requires suppressing the natural tendency to look toward it.
source: Participants had to look away from a suddenly appearing visual stimulus (an antisaccade), which requires to suppress the natural tendency to look toward it (Munoz and Everling, 2004).
evidence: This describes the antisaccade task, supported by citation to Munoz and Everling, 2004.

claim: During the time-window identified by Salinas et al., eye movements were strongly drawn to the location of the visual stimulus, even though this conflicted with current task-goals.
source: During the time-window, Salinas et al. observed that the eye movements were strongly drawn to the location of the visual stimulus, even though this conflicted with current task-goals.
evidence: This describes a specific finding from Salinas et al., 2019.

claim: Salinas et al. interpreted their finding as evidence for an 'attentional vortex', a period in which the endogenous (goal-directed) control of spatial attention was overpowered by the exogenous attraction of spatial attention to the stimulus location.
source: The authors interpreted this finding as evidence for an 'attentional vortex', a period in which the endogenous (goal-directed) control of spatial attention was overpowered by the exogenous attraction of spatial attention to the stimulus location.
evidence: This describes Salinas et al.'s interpretation of their findings.

claim: The interpretation of Salinas et al.'s findings in terms of attention control was hotly debated during eLife's open peer-review.
source: However, this interpretation in terms of attention control was hotly debated during eLife's open peer-review (https://elifesciences.org/articles/46359#SA1).
evidence: This references the peer review discussion, with a URL citation.

claim: It was suggested during peer review that Salinas et al.'s findings reflected a specific visually driven impairment of eye movement control (oculomotor capture), and that 'the link to attention is only inferred'.
source: Given the tight links of vision and eye movements, it was suggested that the findings reflected a specific visually driven impairment of eye movement control (oculomotor capture; e.g., Irwin et al., 2000), and that 'the link to attention is only inferred' (review round 2, point 1).
evidence: This describes a suggestion from peer review, with citation to the review and to Irwin et al., 2000.

claim: Salinas et al. modeled potential mechanisms underlying their findings based on neuronal activity of brain regions specialized in eye movement control.
source: Compatible with the suggestion, Salinas et al. modeled potential mechanisms underlying their findings based on neuronal activity of brain regions specialized in eye movement control (Costello et al., 2013; Seideman et al., 2018; Shankar et al., 2011; Stanford et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes Salinas et al.'s modeling approach, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Salinas et al.'s modeling constrains interpretations to the domain of eye movements and closely related brain mechanisms of spatial attention.
source: Thus, in line with the suggestion, this modeling constrains interpretations to the domain of eye movements and closely related brain mechanisms of spatial attention (Moore and Armstrong, 2003).
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of Salinas et al.'s modeling approach, with citation to Moore and Armstrong, 2003.

claim: Urgency elicits stimulus-driven behavior that can conflict with current goals beyond eye movement control and spatial attention mechanisms.
source: Going even beyond Salinas et al.'s 'attentional vortex', we found that urgency generally elicits stimulus-driven behavior that can conflict with current goals.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by data from both experiments.

claim: In two well-established manual tasks of cognitive control, behavioral responses were dominated by task-irrelevant stimulus information under urgency.
source: In two well-established manual tasks of cognitive control, behavioral responses were dominated by task-irrelevant stimulus information.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: Under urgency, participants could not help but execute stimulus-driven responses that were in clear conflict with their current goals.
source: As a result, participants could not help but execute stimulus-driven responses that were in clear conflict with their current goals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing below-chance performance in incongruent conditions.

claim: Experiment 1 revealed a dominance of stimulus-driven behavior for conflicts of spatial stimulus location.
source: Experiment 1 revealed such a dominance of stimulus-driven behavior for conflicts of spatial stimulus location
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiment 1 using the spatial Stroop task.

claim: Experiment 2 demonstrated the dominance of stimulus-driven behavior for nonspatial cognitive conflicts.
source: and Experiment 2 demonstrated the same pattern even for nonspatial cognitive conflicts.
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiment 2 using the flanker task.

claim: In both experiments, the dominance of stimulus-driven behavior followed trial-to-trial sequence effects that are interpreted as top-down and/or bottom-up modulations of cognitive control mechanisms.
source: In both experiments, the dominance of stimulus-driven behavior followed trial-to-trial sequence effects that are interpreted as top-down and/or bottom-up modulations of cognitive control mechanisms (Egner, 2017; Egner, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing sequence effects and citations to Egner's work on cognitive control.

claim: Urgency temporarily helps external stimuli to overcome (e.g., bypass) the goal-driven cognitive control of action at processing levels extending beyond vision, spatial attention, and eye movement control.
source: As such, these findings uncover that urgency temporarily helps external stimuli to overcome (e.g., bypass) the goal-driven cognitive control of action at processing levels extending beyond vision, spatial attention, and eye movement control (such as levels of prefrontal brain mechanisms; Egner, 2007; Egner and Hirsch, 2005).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, with citations to relevant literature on prefrontal mechanisms.

claim: In the spatial Stroop task, participants had to respond by pressing one of two buttons to indicate whether a target stimulus (an arrow) was pointing left or right.
source: In this task, participants had to respond by pressing one of two buttons to indicate whether a target stimulus, an arrow (see Figure 1), was pointing left or right.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: In the spatial Stroop task, the target arrow could appear either to the left or right of screen center.
source: The target arrow could appear either to the left or right of screen center.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment 1.

claim: In the congruent condition of the spatial Stroop task, the target arrow appeared on the side it was pointing to.
source: In the congruent condition, the target arrow appeared on the side it was pointing to.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment 1.

claim: In the incongruent condition of the spatial Stroop task, the target arrow appeared on the side opposite to where it was pointing to.
source: In the incongruent condition, the target arrow appeared on the side opposite to where it was pointing to.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment 1.

claim: The incongruent condition in spatial Stroop tasks leads to slower reaction times, indicating that the spatial location and the pointing direction of the target arrow produced a cognitive conflict for action.
source: Such a condition has been shown to lead to slower reaction times, indicating that the spatial location and the pointing direction of the target arrow produced a cognitive conflict for action (e.g., Lu and Proctor, 1995; Schneider, 2020, Experiment 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on spatial Stroop effects.

claim: Cognitive control can be quantified by assessing how well cognitive conflict can be resolved.
source: Cognitive control can be quantified by assessing how well this cognitive conflict can be resolved.
evidence: This describes a standard approach in cognitive control research.

claim: Cognitive control is measured by comparing performance in incongruent versus congruent conditions.
source: This is done by measuring how performance suffers in the incongruent condition compared with the congruent condition.
evidence: This describes a standard methodological approach in cognitive control research.

claim: If cognitive control was perfect, performance should be equal in congruent and incongruent conditions.
source: If cognitive control was perfect, performance should be equal in the conditions
evidence: This is a logical inference about what perfect cognitive control would entail.

claim: For worse cognitive control, performance should drop stronger in the incongruent compared with the congruent condition.
source: and for worse cognitive control, performance should drop stronger in the incongruent compared with the congruent condition.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what impaired cognitive control would entail.

claim: The evolution of cognitive control over time was traced using a manipulation of urgency.
source: Harnessing these classic congruency effects, we traced the evolution of cognitive control over time using a manipulation of urgency.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the current study.

claim: In the beginning of a trial, participants fixated a small square in the center of the screen.
source: In the beginning of a trial, participants fixated a small square in the center of the screen.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure, as shown in Figure 1.

claim: The disappearance of the fixation stimulus served as the go-signal, prompting participants to respond after 1 s.
source: The disappearance of this fixation stimulus served as the go-signal, prompting participants to respond after 1 s.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Urgency was manipulated by introducing a gap of different durations after the go-signal and before the target stimulus that indicated the response to be made.
source: Urgency was manipulated by introducing a gap of different durations after the go-signal and before the target stimulus that indicated the response to be made (Salinas et al., 2019; Stanford et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation, with citations to prior work using this approach.

claim: When the duration of the gap is short, urgency should be low because the target appears just after the go-signal, allowing for processing the target in order to prepare the motor response.
source: When the duration of the gap is short, urgency should be low. The target appears just after the go-signal, allowing for processing the target in order to prepare the motor response.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between gap duration and urgency.

claim: When the gap duration is long, urgency should be high because during the gap after the go-signal, the time left for responding is elapsing, but the target specifying the response is still missing.
source: In contrast, when the gap duration is long, urgency should be high. During the gap after the go-signal, the time left for responding is elapsing, but the target specifying the response is still missing.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between gap duration and urgency.

claim: With long gap durations, time-pressure for responding is building up, so that participants must prepare their motor responses before it becomes clear which response has to be chosen.
source: Thus, time-pressure for responding is building up, so that participants must prepare their motor responses before it becomes clear which response has to be chosen.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of long gap durations.

claim: The manipulation of gap duration may have induced urgency as an internal state of participants' cognitive system, as measures assumed to index physiological arousal were found to increase with increasing gap duration.
source: This manipulation may have induced urgency as an internal state of participants' cognitive system, as measures assumed to index physiological arousal were found to increase with increasing gap duration (Appendix 1—figure 2; but see the discussion there).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Appendix 1—figure 2, though with caveats noted.

claim: Raw processing time (RPT) for the target is computed as the time the target was visible within the reaction time (i.e., the reaction time from the go-signal minus the gap duration).
source: Following Salinas et al., 2019, we computed the raw processing time (RPT) for the target as the time the target was visible within the reaction time (i.e., the reaction time from the go-signal minus the gap duration).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach, following Salinas et al., 2019.

claim: For both congruent and incongruent conditions, the temporal evolution of performance was assessed by computing the tachometric function, which is the psychometric function relating performance to RPT.
source: For both conditions, we assessed the temporal evolution of performance by computing the tachometric function, which is the psychometric function relating performance to RPT (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the analytical approach, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The tachometric functions revealed a qualitative difference between the congruent and incongruent condition.
source: This revealed a qualitative difference between the congruent and incongruent condition (and closely replicated a pilot experiment, see Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and replication of a pilot experiment.

claim: In the congruent condition, performance rose monotonously from chance level up to an asymptote at near-perfect performance.
source: In the congruent condition, performance rose monotonously from chance level up to an asymptote at near-perfect performance.
evidence: This describes the pattern observed in the data, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the incongruent condition, the tachometric function started at chance and evolved toward near-perfect performance, but dropped below chance level in a demarcated time-window around an RPT of about 250 ms.
source: In contrast, the tachometric function in the incongruent condition followed a qualitatively different course: While it also started at chance and evolved toward near-perfect performance, it dropped below chance level in a demarcated time-window around an RPT of about 250 ms.
evidence: This describes the pattern observed in the data, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: The maximum drop below chance was lower in the incongruent condition than the congruent condition (p < 0.001).
source: The maximum drop below chance was lower in the incongruent condition than the congruent condition (p < 0.001, permutation test, see Materials and methods; Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis, shown in Figure 2b.

claim: There was a time-window of RPTs in which responses were dominated by the spatial location of the target arrow rather than its pointing direction, even though this violated the task instructions.
source: This reveals that there was a time-window of RPTs in which responses were dominated by the spatial location of the target arrow rather than its pointing direction, even though this violated the task instructions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the below-chance performance in the incongruent condition.

claim: After the time-window of below-chance performance, performance in the incongruent condition recovered up to near-perfect performance, but reached this level much later compared with the congruent condition (the tachometric function was shifted to the right for ~80 ms).
source: After this time-window, performance in the incongruent condition recovered up to near-perfect performance, but reached this level much later compared with the congruent condition (i.e., the tachometric function was shifted to the right for ~80 ms, see Figure 2a).
evidence: This describes a pattern observed in the data, as shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Cognitive control mechanisms eventually resolved the competition between stimulus information and current goals in favor of the goals, but this resolution required a substantial amount of processing time.
source: This indicates that cognitive control mechanisms eventually resolved the competition between stimulus information and current goals in favor of the goals, but that this resolution required a substantial amount of processing time.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the recovery of performance after the below-chance period.

claim: One hallmark of cognitive control is that it is dynamic: Humans can adapt or learn to compensate cognitive conflicts.
source: One hallmark of cognitive control is that it is dynamic: Humans can adapt or learn to compensate cognitive conflicts (Botvinick et al., 2001; Egner, 2007; Hommel et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on cognitive control.

claim: Performance decrements due to cognitive conflicts are less pronounced following trials with cognitive conflict (incongruent trials) than trials without such conflict.
source: so that performance decrements are less pronounced following trials with cognitive conflict (incongruent trials) than trials without such conflict.
evidence: This describes a well-established pattern in cognitive control research.

claim: Performance dropped more strongly below chance level in the incongruent condition when the preceding trial was congruent rather than incongruent (p < 0.001).
source: We discovered that this was also the case for our urgency-based effects: Performance dropped more strongly below chance level in the incongruent condition when the preceding trial was congruent rather than incongruent (p < 0.001, permutation test, Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis, shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The drops of performance below chance exhibit the same trial-to-trial modulations of established congruency effects.
source: Thus, the drops of performance below chance exhibit the same trial-to-trial modulations of established congruency effects.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the sequence effects observed in the data.

claim: The pattern of trial-to-trial modulations offers converging evidence that established mechanisms of cognitive control are involved.
source: This pattern of results offers converging evidence that indeed the established mechanisms of cognitive control are involved (e.g., Egner, 2017).
evidence: This is an inference from the data pattern, with citation to Egner, 2017.

claim: The results of the spatial Stroop task reveal a demarcated time-window along the urgency axis in which cognitive control is overcome, so that responses cannot be based on the symbolic information of the target arrow but are involuntarily based on the spatial location of the target.
source: Taken together, the results of spatial Stroop task of Experiment 1 reveal a demarcated time-window along the urgency axis in which cognitive control is overcome, so that responses cannot be based on the symbolic information of the target arrow (i.e., its pointing direction), but are involuntarily (against task instructions) based on the spatial location of the target.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from Experiment 1 data.

claim: Salinas et al. observed similar effects for saccadic eye movements, in which urgency led to a time-window in which saccades were involuntarily drawn toward rather than against a suddenly appearing target.
source: Salinas et al. observed similar effects for saccadic eye movements, in which urgency led to a time-window in which saccades were involuntarily drawn toward rather than against (as per the instructions) a suddenly appearing target.
evidence: This describes findings from Salinas et al., 2019.

claim: The findings suggest that the dominance of stimulus information over cognitive control is not limited to the capture of eye movements by sudden stimuli.
source: Thus, the present findings suggest that such a dominance of stimulus information over cognitive control is not limited to the capture of eye movements by sudden stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the current findings with Salinas et al.'s work.

claim: Cognitive control is overcome (e.g., bypassed) by stimuli also in manual decision tasks.
source: Rather, cognitive control is overcome (e.g., bypassed) by the stimuli also in manual decision tasks.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the data of Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, cognitive conflicts arose from the task-irrelevant spatial location of the target stimulus.
source: In Experiment 1, cognitive conflicts arose from the task-irrelevant spatial location of the target stimulus.
evidence: This describes the design of Experiment 1.

claim: The dominance over cognitive control could be limited to spatial cognitive conflicts.
source: Thus, the dominance over cognitive control could be limited to such spatial cognitive conflicts.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential limitations of the findings from Experiment 1.

claim: Experiment 2 was performed to test whether the findings translated to nonspatial types of cognitive conflict.
source: Therefore, we performed Experiment 2 to test whether our present findings translated to nonspatial types of cognitive conflict.
evidence: This describes the rationale for Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, the paradigm and trial sequence were similar to Experiment 1.
source: In Experiment 2, cognitive control was assessed using a flanker task (Eriksen and Eriksen, 1974; Ridderinkhof et al., 2021). The paradigm and trial sequence were similar to the one of Experiment 1.
evidence: This describes the design of Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, the target arrow always appeared at screen center.
source: However, here the target arrow always appeared at screen center.
evidence: This describes the design of Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, the target was flanked by four distractor arrows.
source: The target was flanked by four distractor arrows.
evidence: This describes the design of Experiment 2.

claim: In the congruent condition of Experiment 2, the distractors pointed in the same direction as the target arrow, so that there was no cognitive conflict.
source: In the congruent condition, the distractors pointed in the same direction as the target arrow, so that there was no cognitive conflict.
evidence: This describes the design of Experiment 2.

claim: In the incongruent condition of Experiment 2, the distractors pointed into the opposite direction as the target, thus providing conflicting information as to which response had to be executed.
source: In contrast, in the incongruent condition, the distractors pointed into the opposite direction as the target, thus providing conflicting information as to which response had to be executed.
evidence: This describes the design of Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, the conflict was not spatial in the sense that it was due to the target's spatial location, because the target always appeared at screen center.
source: In contrast to Experiment 1, as the target always appeared at screen center, the conflict was not spatial in the sense that it was due to the target's spatial location.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of the conflict in Experiment 2.

claim: Results of Experiment 2 revealed the same pattern as in Experiment 1.
source: Results revealed the same pattern as in Experiment 1.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, performance monotonously rose from chance to near-perfect performance with increasing RPT in the congruent condition.
source: Performance monotonously rose from chance to near-perfect performance with increasing RPT in the congruent condition (Figure 2d).
evidence: This describes the pattern observed in the data, as shown in Figure 2d.

claim: In Experiment 2, within a demarcated time-window of RPTs, performance dropped below chance level in the incongruent condition (p < 0.001).
source: In contrast, within a demarcated time-window of RPTs, performance dropped below chance level in the incongruent condition (p < 0.001, permutation test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: Even though the type of cognitive conflict was nonspatial in Experiment 2, urgency resulted in the temporary dominance of responses by stimulus information from the distractors over goal-driven cognitive control.
source: Thus, even though the type of cognitive conflict was nonspatial, urgency resulted in the temporary dominance of responses by stimulus information from the distractors over goal-driven cognitive control.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, after the time-window of performance drop, performance in the incongruent condition recovered, but this required additional processing time (the tachometric function was shifted to the right for ~120 ms).
source: As in Experiment 1, after the time-window of this performance drop, performance in the incongruent condition recovered, but this required additional processing time (i.e., the tachometric function was shifted to the right for ~120 ms, see Figure 2d).
evidence: This describes a pattern observed in the data, as shown in Figure 2d.

claim: In Experiment 2, cognitive control mechanisms eventually enacted goal-driven responses rather than stimulus-driven ones, but for this the mechanisms needed a substantial amount of processing time.
source: Thus, again, cognitive control mechanisms eventually enacted goal-driven responses rather than stimulus-driven ones, but for this the mechanisms needed a substantial amount of processing time.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the recovery of performance after the below-chance period in Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, the dominance of stimulus information was subject to trial-to-trial sequence effects typical for cognitive control.
source: As in Experiment 1, this dominance of stimulus information was subject to the trial-to-trial sequence effects typical for cognitive control.
evidence: This describes a pattern observed in the data of Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, performance fell below chance more strongly after trials with no conflict (congruent trials) compared to trials with conflict (incongruent trials; p = 0.019).
source: That is, the performance fell below chance more strongly after trials with no conflict (congruent trials) compared to trials with conflict (incongruent trials; p = 0.019, permutation test, Figure 2f).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis, shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The results of Experiment 2 suggest that urgency elicits a circumscribed time-window in which stimulus-driven behavior overcomes cognitive control also for nonspatial cognitive conflicts.
source: Taken together, the results of Experiment 2 suggest that urgency elicits a circumscribed time-window in which stimulus-driven behavior overcomes cognitive control also for nonspatial cognitive conflicts.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from Experiment 2 data.

claim: Urgency elicited a time-window in which the capability to resolve cognitive conflicts between current goals and stimulus information was lost.
source: Urgency elicited a time-window in which the capability to resolve cognitive conflicts between current goals and stimulus information was lost.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from both experiments.

claim: During the time-window elicited by urgency, participants' responses were dominated by stimulus information, forcing them to execute stimulus-driven responses against their current task-goals.
source: During this time-window, participants' responses were dominated by stimulus information, forcing them to execute stimulus-driven responses against their current task-goals.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from both experiments.

claim: The pattern of results closely resembles the effects of abruptly appearing visual stimuli on saccadic eye movements found by Salinas et al., 2019.
source: This pattern of results closely resembles the effects of abruptly appearing visual stimuli on saccadic eye movements found by Salinas et al., 2019.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with prior work.

claim: The present findings reveal that urgency effects have more wide-ranging implications than previously thought.
source: However, the present findings reveal that these urgency effects have more wide-ranging implications than previously thought.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current findings.

claim: Rather than causing a limited visual–oculomotor phenomenon, urgency seems to force stimulus-driven behavior overcoming cognitive control more generally.
source: Rather than causing a limited visual–oculomotor phenomenon, urgency seems to force stimulus-driven behavior overcoming cognitive control more generally.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current findings.

claim: Stimulus-driven behavior was temporarily enforced in two manual tasks, showing that this phenomenon is not restricted to saccadic eye movements.
source: Stimulus-driven behavior was temporarily enforced in two manual tasks, showing that this phenomenon is not restricted to saccadic eye movements.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the data of both experiments.

claim: Compared with eye movements, the effect of urgency on stimulus-driven behavior appeared for longer RPTs, in line with the generally longer reaction times for manual movements compared with eye movements.
source: Compared with eye movements, this effect appeared for longer RPTs, in line with the generally longer reaction times for manual movements compared with eye movements.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the current findings with Salinas et al.'s work, drawing on general knowledge about reaction times.

claim: The phenomenon of urgency-induced stimulus dominance was found for cognitive conflicts in which the spatial location of stimuli conflicted with their task-relevant features (Experiment 1).
source: We found the phenomenon for cognitive conflicts in which the spatial location of stimuli conflicted with their task-relevant features (Experiment 1).
evidence: This summarizes the findings from Experiment 1.

claim: The finding in Experiment 1 is in line with Salinas et al.'s interpretation that urgency caused an irresistibly strong capture of saccadic eye movements by the visual stimulus (oculomotor capture) in their antisaccade task.
source: This is in line with Salinas et al.'s interpretation that urgency caused an irresistibly strong capture of saccadic eye movements by the visual stimulus (oculomotor capture; Theeuwes, 2014) in their antisaccade task.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to Salinas et al.'s interpretation, with citation to Theeuwes, 2014.

claim: Given the tight links of eye movement control and spatial attention, oculomotor capture should not only attract saccades (overt attention), but also covert spatial attention (without saccadic eye movements) prioritizing the target's location for perception.
source: Given the tight links of eye movement control and spatial attention (Deubel and Schneider, 1996; Moore and Armstrong, 2003; Rolfs et al., 2011), such a capture should not only attract saccades (overt attention), but also covert spatial attention (without saccadic eye movements) prioritizing the target's location for perception (Carrasco, 2011; Theeuwes, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about the relationship between eye movements and spatial attention, supported by multiple citations.

claim: For Experiment 1, prioritization of stimulus location by spatial attention could have provoked manual responses that were compatible in their spatial organization.
source: For Experiment 1, such a prioritization of stimulus location could have provoked manual responses that were compatible in their spatial organization (Lu and Proctor, 1995).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the findings in Experiment 1, with citation to Lu and Proctor, 1995.

claim: The findings of Experiment 1 could be explained by assuming mechanisms similar to those implicated in Salinas et al.'s eye movement paradigm.

claim: Action control happens faster if it is driven by stimulus information rather than cognitive control mechanisms enacting current goals.
source: Thus, this underscores that action control happens faster if it is driven by stimulus information rather than cognitive control mechanisms enacting current goals.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that goal-directed responses required additional processing time.

claim: In both experiments, the dominance of stimulus information over cognitive control was stronger after trials without conflict than trials with conflict.
source: Furthermore, in both experiments, the dominance of stimulus information over cognitive control was stronger after trials without conflict than trials with conflict.

claim: The precise nature of top-down and bottom-up influences underlying trial-to-trial modulations is still debated.

claim: The pattern of trial-to-trial modulations offers corroborating evidence that established cognitive control mechanisms were involved that are sensitive to these modulations.

claim: The findings uncover that urgency temporarily helps external stimuli to overcome cognitive control not only in saccadic eye movements and spatial attention, but in goal-directed behavior more generally.

evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on data from both experiments.

claim: In an urgent task, the motor plans for the response alternatives are active after the go-signal for responding, even if the stimulus indicating which response should be made has not yet appeared.
source: In an urgent task, the motor plans for the response alternatives are active after the go-signal for responding, even if the stimulus indicating which response should be made has not yet appeared (Salinas et al., 2019; Stanford et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about urgent tasks, supported by citations to Salinas et al., 2019 and Stanford et al., 2010.

claim: In urgent tasks, the motor plans are both active and compete, and this competition must be resolved 'on-the-fly' using incoming visual information.
source: Thus, the motor plans are both active and compete, and this competition must be resolved 'on-the-fly' using incoming visual information.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of motor planning in urgent tasks.

claim: Competition between motor plans can be resolved by pausing or accelerating the motor plans based on either the most salient stimulus information or based on goal-relevant stimulus information, by means of cognitive control mechanisms.
source: This can be achieved by pausing or accelerating the motor plans (Salinas et al., 2019; Salinas and Stanford, 2018) based on either the most salient stimulus information (in Experiment 1, the location of an abrupt onset, in Experiment 2 the information provided by the majority of the stimuli) or based on goal-relevant stimulus information, by means of cognitive control mechanisms.
evidence: This describes potential mechanisms for resolving motor plan competition, with citations to Salinas et al., 2019 and Salinas and Stanford, 2018.

claim: In urgent situations, salient stimulus information could have privileged access to the motor plans because the cognitive control mechanisms are transiently interrupted that would otherwise filter out the information.
source: Now, in urgent situations, salient stimulus information could have privileged access to the motor plans because the cognitive control mechanisms are transiently interrupted that would otherwise filter out the information (and prevent it from biasing the motor plans).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism by which urgency affects cognitive control.

claim: The privileged access of salient stimuli to motor plans may be part of an adaptive mechanism that allows salient stimuli to directly affect ongoing motor plans to enable that responses are delivered promptly.

evidence: This is a speculation about the adaptive function of the observed phenomenon, with citations to Salinas and Stanford, 2018 and Stanford and Salinas, 2021.

claim: The time-pressure to respond (the gap duration), and thus urgency, was associated with two indices of physiological arousal, namely pupil size and saccade peak velocity.

claim: Urgency-induced arousal would be similar to temporary states of phasic alertness, which occur after warning signals and speed up cognitive information processing.

evidence: This is a speculation about how arousal might mediate urgency effects.

claim: Shortened competition time could cause the salient information with its stronger neuronal representations to almost immediately decide the competition in its favor.

evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism by which urgency affects motor plan competition.

source: No time would be left for cognitive control mechanisms to counteract the influence of this information (irrespective of whether cognitive control was transiently interrupted).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism by which urgency affects cognitive control.

claim: The proposed mechanism would be in line with the physiologically inspired computational model by Salinas et al., 2019, which explains the dominance of stimulus information over the cognitive control of saccades by a period in which faster exogenous signals already affect motor plans while slower endogenous signals have not yet been processed up to this level.
source: This would be in line with the physiologically inspired computational model by Salinas et al., 2019, which explains the dominance of stimulus information over the cognitive control of saccades by a period in which faster exogenous signals already affect motor plans while slower endogenous signals have not yet been processed up to this level.

claim: The dominance of stimulus information over cognitive control does not indicate that cognitive control mechanisms fail.
